newsitem.title: USA: French minister says against letting deficit rise.
newsitem.headline: French minister says against letting deficit rise.

text.p: French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said on Saturday he was against allowing France's budget deficit to rise significantly.

He told reporters after a meeting of the Group of Seven rich nations that he could not comment in detail on the deficit until the results of an audit being carried out by the new Socialist-led government were ready in mid-July.
"If the audit shows a sizeable deficit, we must look then at what measures need to be taken," he said.

He had been asked whether France's European partners had shown any worries about the French budget deficit, which newspapers have suggested could be well above the Maastricht treaty criteria limiting it to three percent of gross domestic product.

"If (the deficit) is sizeable, I would be first to be worried before the others," Strauss-Kahn said, noting that large budget deficits would be bad for the French economy even independently of Maastricht treaty requirements.
He noted that Prime Minister Lionel Jospin had said during his election campaign that he had no intention of increasing the deficit.
France's new government has said it wants a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht treaty.

The treaty itself allows the European Union to take account of a trend towards a deficit/GDP ratio of three percent in deciding which countries qualify to join a single currency in 1999, though Germany has pushed for a strict interpretation, reducing the ratio to exactly 3.0 percent.
Asked about what level the French government would consider acceptable, Strauss-Kahn said, "our position is still the same on this -- the treaty".
He added that Jospin had made clear his determination that France would join the single European currency in 1999 and said he saw no reason to doubt this.
